title: When the Archive Falls Anew
premise: Freya Joubert smuggles memories—recorded human experience—past orbital customs in her patched-together freighter, the only witness to the slow abandonment of Meridian Colony, which corporate archives claim never existed. When she intercepts a distress signal in a language extinct since the Vellish Purge, she traces it to a hidden settlement of descendants who preserved their forbidden culture in off-grid memory vaults—the same vaults a salvage consortium now plans to erase, along with everyone in them. To prove the coming massacre and the original one two centuries past, Freya must smuggle not contraband but testimony itself, risking the found family she built among the forgotten. In the end, she broadcasts the archive to every receiver in the system, sacrificing her anonymity and nearly her life, so that Meridian's dead—and its living—are remembered whether the powers that be consent or not.
about_author: Tamsin Delacroix is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing records of communities erased by redevelopment, an experience that haunts everything she writes. She lives somewhere with unreliable internet and writes science fiction about the people history tries to lose.

chapters.title: Contraband of the Heart
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A routine smuggling run through orbital customs: Freya hides stolen memories—a dying fisherman's last season, a mother's lullabies—in her ship's coolant lines while customs drones scan for data-contraband. Establishes her trade, her loneliness, and her quiet habit of recording Meridian Colony's decay. Emotional beat: competent isolation, the comfort of being unseen.

chapters.title: The Colony That Isn't
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya docks at Meridian to deliver supplies to the dwindling settlement and visits old Marta Okonkwo, keeper of the colony's unofficial oral record. Corporate census ships pass without stopping; officially, Meridian was decommissioned forty years ago. Emotional beat: tenderness sharpened by dread—Freya realizes she may be the only archivist of a place being erased in real time.

chapters.title: Signal in a Dead Tongue
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In deep space between runs, Freya's salvaged receiver catches a repeating distress signal in Vellish, a language exterminated during the Purge two centuries ago. Her grandmother's lullabies were half Vellish; she recognizes it in her bones. Emotional beat: uncanny grief—grief for something she thought was already fully lost, reaching out from the dark.

chapters.title: Dead Drop Decisions
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya weighs the signal against her survival rules: never follow distress calls, never become visible. Her fence, Juno Reyes, warns that anything Vellish-flagged will draw the attention of Halcyon Salvage Consortium, which holds the colonial charter. Emotional beat: fear wrestling with inheritance—she cannot pretend she didn't hear her ancestors' tongue calling.

chapters.title: The Vault Beneath the Ice
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Following triangulated coordinates, Freya lands on a frozen moon and finds a concealed settlement: three hundred descendants of Purge survivors living around geothermal vents, guarding memory vaults of forbidden recordings. Their speaker, Elder Sefa Vell, greets her in accented trade-tongue. Emotional beat: awe and vertigo—Freya has spent her life invisible, and here is a whole world that hid better than she ever did.

chapters.title: What the Vaults Hold
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Sefa shows Freya the vaults: centuries of Vellish song, law, names—proof the Purge massacre happened, proof the archives lie. But the vaults are failing, and Halcyon survey drones have been circling for months. Emotional beat: guarded hope curdling into urgency as Sefa realizes this stranger may be their only link to the outside.

chapters.title: A Boy Who Remembers Forward
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, mostly young Tam Vell. Freya meets Tam, a teenager who has memorized ten thousand songs and dreams of leaving. He attaches himself to her, insisting she take his recorded memories out if the worst happens. Emotional beat: reluctant affection—Freya recognizes her younger self in him and hates how much she cares already.

chapters.title: Halcyon's Ledger
chapters.summary: Consortium surveyor Dain Kessler's POV. Kessler discovers the settlement on his thermal scans and files a report recommending 'site clearance'—the moon sits atop rare-earth deposits, and the charter's extinction clauses make erasure legal and profitable. Emotional beat: banal evil—Kessler feels nothing but professional satisfaction at a tidy report.

chapters.title: Terms of Smuggling
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The settlement votes to trust Freya with copies of the vault core: the full archive of Vellish memory, too large to hide in coolant lines. She'll need new methods, new routes, and allies—which means revealing herself. Emotional beat: terror of exposure transformed into resolve; invisibility was always a kind of death anyway.

chapters.title: Juno's Price
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya confesses everything to Juno, who reveals she's been skimming Freya's runs to pay down a debt to Halcyon—and that Halcyon now owns markers on both of them. Juno agrees to help anyway. Emotional beat: betrayal and forgiveness braided together; found family means loving people who have failed you.

chapters.title: The First Copy Runs
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya moves the first archive shard through customs disguised as entertainment media, nearly caught by a new Halcyon-backed scanner that reads emotional resonance in stored memory. She escapes by burning a decoy cache of her own childhood recordings. Emotional beat: loss as payment—she is literally spending her past to buy the future of someone else's.

chapters.title: Kessler Closes In
chapters.summary: Kessler's POV. Kessler traces the anomalous data traffic back toward the ice moon and requests a 'salvage assessment' team—private security with demolition licenses. He also flags Freya's ship registry. Emotional beat: tightening noose; the reader sees the machinery of erasure assembling while the settlers prepare a harvest festival.

chapters.title: Festival of Names
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The settlement holds its festival, reciting the names of the Purge dead into the vaults. Freya, attending openly for the first time, is given a Vellish name: Freya-of-the-Carrying. Emotional beat: belonging—brief, warm, and doomed-feeling, the calm before the storm made explicit when a drone passes overhead during the final recitation.

chapters.title: Evacuation Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Sefa confronts the math: the settlement's aging shuttle can carry sixty people, maybe eighty. Three hundred live here. The elders debate scattering versus standing; Sefa secretly begins choosing who goes. Emotional beat: the terrible arithmetic of love—who do you save when you can't save everyone?

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Juno alerts Freya: Halcyon has issued a clearance order for the moon, scheduled in nine days, papered over as a mining accident waiting to happen. Freya races back through a customs blockade to warn the settlement. Emotional beat: desperation at speed—every chapter of caution traded for one reckless, necessary run.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The settlement mobilizes: copying what the vaults can still hold, packing the shuttle, arguing, weeping. Freya proposes the impossible alternative—if they can't all leave, make the massacre undeniable: broadcast the archive live, from the ground, as it happens. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into defiance; the plan is insane and it is theirs.

chapters.title: The Relay Gambit
chapters.summary: Freya and Juno's POV. Freya and Juno hijack a decommissioned comm relay above the moon, rigging it to rebroadcast the vault feed system-wide, unjammable. Kessler's security fleet arrives early. Emotional beat: breathless competence under fire—two smugglers and a dead satellite against a corporation's private navy.

chapters.title: What the Records Say
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. As security teams land, Tam leads the youngest children into the deep vaults with portable cores, following escape tunnels his grandfather dug for exactly this day. Above, Sefa stands at the settlement gate and speaks the elders' refusal in Vellish, recorded by every drone present. Emotional beat: courage as inheritance—the children carry forward what the elders refuse to abandon.

chapters.title: The Massacre Broadcast
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Climax. Halcyon forces fire on the settlement; the relay carries every second of it—screams, songs, Sefa's voice—to millions of receivers. Freya, wounded, keeps the feed alive from her ship while Juno holds the relay physically together. Emotional beat: horror and triumph indivisible—they cannot stop the massacre, but they make it unforgettable, undeniable, eternal.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Unedited
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The broadcast detonates across the system: protests, investigations, Halcyon's charter suspended pending inquiry. Two hundred and eleven survive, including Tam and most of the children. Kessler, facing tribunal, insists he only filed paperwork. Emotional beat: hollow victory—justice arriving late, priced in blood, yet real.

chapters.title: The Archive Falls Anew
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. On a station granted to the survivors, Tam opens the new vault—not hidden this time, but public, its doors glass, its contents free to any who ask. He records the first entry: the names of the dead, then the names of the living. Emotional beat: grief becoming foundation; secrecy kept them alive, openness keeps them real.

chapters.title: Freya-of-the-Carrying
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya, scarred and famous against her will, prepares for a supply run to the next forgotten colony—her hold full not of contraband but of blank recording cores, offered freely. Juno crews with her; Tam sends a song as she clears the dock. Emotional beat: quiet continuation—she was never really invisible, and now she chooses to be seen, carrying other people's memories home.
